'''''Silene dioica''''' ([[synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''Melandrium rubrum''), known as '''red campion'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> and '''red catchfly''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SIDI4|taxon=Silene dioica|accessdate=14 November 2015}}</ref> is a [[herbaceous]] [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Caryophyllaceae]], native to Europe and introduced to the Americas.

==Description==
It is a [[biennial plant|biennial]] or [[perennial plant]], which grows to {{Convert|30–90|cm|abbr=off}} tall, with branching stems. The deep green [[leaves]] are in [[opposite leaves|opposite]] and [[Glossary of botanical terms|decussate]] pairs, simple acute ovate, {{Convert|3–8|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long with an untoothed margin; both the leaves and stems of the plant are hairy and slightly sticky. The upper leaves are stalkless.<ref name="Stace" />

Blooming from May to October, the unscented [[flower]]s are dark pink to red, each {{Convert|1.8–2.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} across. There are five [[petals]] which are deeply notched at the end, narrowed at the base and all go into an urn-shaped [[sepal|calyx]].  As indicated by the specific name, male and female flowers are borne on separate plants ([[Dioecy|dioecious]]), the male with 10 [[stamens]] and a 10-veined calyx, the female with 5 styles and a 20-veined calyx.<ref name="Stace" />

The fruit, produced from July onwards, is an ovoid capsule containing numerous seeds, opening at the apex by 10 teeth which curve back.<ref name="Stace" />

==Taxonomy==
Plants of ''Silene latifolia'' × ''Silene dioica'' = ''Silene'' × ''hampeana'' that are fertile [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]] with the closely related white campion (''[[Silene latifolia]]'') are common in some areas. They may have paler pink flowers and be intermediate between the two species in other characters.<ref name="Stace">{{cite book |last=Stace |first=C. A. |url=https://archive.org/details/newflorabritishi00stac |title=New Flora of the British Isles |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2010 |isbn=9780521707725 |edition=Third |location=Cambridge, U.K. |pages=[https://archive.org/details/newflorabritishi00stac/page/n508 473] |url-access=limited |authorlink=Stace, C. A.}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Silene dioica'' is native to northern and central Europe and is locally abundant throughout the [[British Isles]].<ref>Clapham, A.R., Tutin, T.G. and Warburg, E.F. 1962. ''Flora of the British Isles.'' Cambridge University Press.</ref> It is generally common in [[Northern Ireland]],<ref>Hackney, P.(Ed) 1992. ''Stewart & Corry's Flora of the North-east of Ireland.'' Third Edition Institute of Irish Studies, The Queen's University of Belfast. {{ISBN|0-85389-446-9}}</ref> but rare elsewhere in [[Ireland]].<ref>Webb, D.A., Parnell, J. and Doogue, D. 1998. ''An Irish Flora.'' Seventh Revised Edition. Dundalgan Press (W. Tempest) Ltd. Dundalk. {{ISBN|0-85221-131-7}}</ref> It is common on the [[Isle of Man]].<ref name="Moore">{{cite book |last=Moore |first=A.W. |authorlink=Arthur William Moore |year=1924 |publisher=Oxford University Press |url=http://www.isle-of-man.com/manxnotebook/fulltext/am1924/index.htm |title=A Vocabulary of the Anglo-Manx Dialect}}</ref> It has been introduced in Iceland, Canada, the US, and Argentina.<ref name="157239-1" />

Red campion grows in roadsides, [[woodland]]s, and rocky slopes.  It prefers to grow on damp, non-acid soils.<ref>[http://www.the-tree.org.uk/EnchantedForest/WoodlandFlowers/campion.htm EnchantedForest: Red Campion] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060521175556/http://www.the-tree.org.uk/EnchantedForest/WoodlandFlowers/campion.htm |date=2006-05-21 }}</ref>

==Ecology==
[[File:The larva of Hadena bicruris is feeding on the seeds of Red Campion (Silene dioica).jpg|right|thumb|A ''Lychnis'' moth caterpillar feeding on the seeds of red campion (''Silene dioica'')|255x255px]]
The flowers are frequently visited by flies such as ''[[Rhingia campestris]]''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Van Der Kooi |first1=C. J. |last2=Pen |first2=I. |last3=Staal |first3=M. |last4=Stavenga |first4=D. G. |last5=Elzenga |first5=J. T. M. |year=2015 |title=Competition for pollinators and intra-communal spectral dissimilarity of flowers |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/273158762 |journal=Plant Biology |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=56–62 |doi=10.1111/plb.12328 |pmid=25754608|hdl=11370/caee8d0d-9724-4056-9d45-93162a5a7afc |hdl-access=free }}</ref> The [[nectar]] of the flowers is utilised by [[bumblebees]] and [[butterflies]], and several species of [[moth]] feed on the [[foliage]].

The flowers of red-campion along with a number of other Caryophyllaceae members, are very susceptible to a [[smut (fungus)|smut]] infection. In this case by ''[[Microbotryum silenes-dioicae]]'' known as anther-smut<ref>{{cite journal|publisher=NCBI|title=Distribution of the anther-smut pathogen Microbotryum on species of the Caryophyllaceae|date=July 2010|pmc=3487183|last1=Hood|first1=M. E.|last2=Mena-Alí|first2=J. I.|last3=Gibson|first3=A. K.|last4=Oxelman|first4=B.|last5=Giraud|first5=T.|last6=Yockteng|first6=R.|last7=Arroyo|first7=M. T.|last8=Conti|first8=F.|last9=Pedersen|first9=A. B.|last10=Gladieux|first10=P.|last11=Antonovics|first11=J.|journal=The New Phytologist|volume=187|issue=1|pages=217–229|doi=10.1111/j.1469-8137.2010.03268.x|pmid=20406409}}</ref> which appears as a mass of brown spores in the mouth of the flower where the anthers would normally be.

==Cultivation==
This plant is used as an ornamental perennial flower for the perennial border.  One particularly notable variety is a hot pink, double flowered variety with deep green leaves called 'Firefly'.

==Medicinal and culinary uses==
The young leaves and flowers of red campion are edible, although cooking or blanching is recommended to remove the bitter aftertaste.<ref>[https://www.eatweeds.co.uk/red-campion-silene-dioica Eat Weeds by Robin Halford]</ref><ref>[https://totallywilduk.co.uk/2023/12/20/red-campion/ Totally wild UK]</ref>

[[Nicholas Culpeper]] recommended red campion for the treatment of [[wart]]s, [[Corn (pathology)|corns]], [[kidney disease]], [[internal bleeding]], [[insect sting]]s, and [[adder]] bites.<ref>[https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Culpeper_s_English_Physician_and_Complet/ZUMnTnBDIMAC?gbpv=1 Nicholas Culpeper, English physician 1798, page 110]</ref>

==In culture==
On the Isle of Man, it is known as "blaa ny ferrishyn" or "fairy flower", and there is a local taboo against picking it.<ref name="Moore" />

In the [[Catholic Church]], red campion flowers are associated with the [[Jesuit]] martyr [[Edmund Campion]].<ref>[https://www.homeopathyschool.com/the-school/provings/red-campion/ Homeopathy school]</ref>
